entry.evidence: the paleoseismic history of many major faults, in terms of recurrence intervals of destructive earthquakes, their magnitude, displacement, and slip rates is poorly understood

sequences.source_document: Mozafari et al. 2022, publisher XML text and PDF

steps.action: States that recurrence intervals, magnitudes and slips of western Anatolian normal faults are poorly constrained and that historical, instrumental and archaeoseismic records are too short.
steps.quote: for long-term seismic modeling, both a better temporal resolution of earthquakes and longer temporal record are required

steps.action: Takes from published work the expectation that episodic exhumation yields cusps and convex segments in 36Cl concentration profiles along a carbonate scarp.
steps.quote: 36Cl concentrations would theoretically display several cusps that indicate periods of high seismic activity

steps.action: Designs the study: samples two new key faults (Rahmiye, Ören) on the northern and southern boundaries of the extensional province and reanalyses 370 published samples from five faults with the same approach.
steps.quote: we improved the seismic datasets of western Anatolia based on cosmogenic 36Cl by studying two new major faults in detail

steps.action: Summarizes the authors' earlier 36Cl reconstructions of the Manastır, Mugırtepe, Kalafat, Yavansu and Priene-Sazlı faults, with re-estimated slip rates.
steps.quote: Two seismic events were reconstructed at ca. 3.5 and 2 ka

steps.action: Examines scarp outcrops along both faults and selects sites with minimal weathering, away from relay zones, river channels and structural boundaries.
steps.quote: We examined a number of scarp outcrops along [...] in the Gediz-Alaşehir Graben and Ören fault

steps.action: Excludes, from field geomorphology, non-tectonic exhumation of the scarps by hill-slope movement, creep or landslide.
steps.quote: exclude any possibility of fault scarp exhumation by any erosional process

steps.action: Samples continuous 15 cm wide strips (87 slabs over 6.5 m at Rahmiye, 127 over 12 m at Ören), measures scarp geometry and colluvium density in the field, and locates the ground line.
steps.quote: a total of 87 samples were collected from the scarp along a ca. 6.5 m high sampling profile

steps.action: Checks the ground line, set from field evidence of recent colluvium removal, against an extrapolation of the colluvium dip; the two give the same level.
steps.quote: Both approaches revealed the same level for the ground line

steps.action: Processes the samples chemically (leaching, isotope dilution, AgCl targets, S removal) and measures total Cl and 36Cl by AMS at ETH Zurich, with major and trace elements by ICP-MS.
steps.quote: The concentrations of total Cl and 36Cl were measured from a single target at the ETH AMS facility using an isotope dilution method

steps.action: Corrects for full process blanks run with each batch of 15 samples and for sulfur; cites the lab's CoCal-N intercomparison agreement.
steps.quote: the contribution of the blank correction to the measured ratios was less than 1%

steps.action: Maps the escarpments and records several scarp levels, two weathering patterns on the Rahmiye surface pointing to stepwise exhumation, preserved corrugations, and Roman excavations.
steps.quote: Two different patterns of weathering, which points to a stepwise exhumation are visible on the fault surface.

steps.action: Fits the 36Cl profiles with FSDT Monte Carlo over 3 to 5 (Rahmiye) and 3 to 6 (Ören) event scenarios, each run more than 100,000 times; selects the lowest chi-square/RMSw/AICc solutions (3 and 4 events) and computes incremental and average slip rates.
steps.quote: A scenario of three seismic events for the Rahmiye fault was populated with 102,408 simulations and provided the best fit solution

steps.action: Computes the expected magnitudes and displacements from fault length with the Pavlides & Caputo (2004) and Wells & Coppersmith (1994) empirical relations, independently of the modeling.
steps.quote: Regardless of modeling, but based on its length of 7 km, the Rahmiye fault can produce an earthquake of magnitude 6.0–6.2

steps.action: Rejects the possibility that the Rahmiye exposure was built by many small, closely timed slips on a 7 km fault, citing the absence of such sequences in records and the continuous dissolution marks.
steps.quote: We exclude this possibility because the occurrence of such repeated seismic activity e.g. over ten earthquakes in short time interval is not known

steps.action: Faced with the mismatch between the few-centimetre slip expected for a 7 km fault and the modeled metres of slip, revises the auxiliary fault length by treating Rahmiye as the extension of the 40 km Akselendi fault.
steps.quote: suggests that the Rahmiye fault should be an extension of the Akselendi fault

steps.action: Compares the magnitudes required by the modeled slips (Table 4) with the theoretical length-based magnitudes and slips (Table 3) to judge plausibility.
steps.quote: both are compared with the theoretical magnitude and slip that can be generated by these faults

steps.action: Supports the youngest Rahmiye event height with independent field evidence: an abrupt weathering change and cross-cutting of dissolution marks by Roman-age excavations, implying exhumation before 2 ka.
steps.quote: supported by the field observation of an abrupt change in weathering features below this level

steps.action: Reinterprets the modeled events as possibly clusters of closely timed earthquakes of magnitude 6.6 to 7.1 rather than single ruptures.
steps.quote: not necessarily characterized by single earthquakes, but also clustering earthquakes

steps.action: Pools the modeled event ages of all seven faults in P-CAAT probability plots and groups them by time correlation into activity phases.
steps.quote: We used P-CAAT (Dortch et al., 35) to plot and evaluate the reconstructed seismic events ages

steps.action: Keeps four regional activity phases (ca. 8, 6, 4, 2 ka), caused by clustered earthquakes on several faults with about 2000-year recurrence, while caveating the incompleteness of the record.
steps.quote: clustering earthquakes of several faults with a recurrence interval of approximately 2000 years

steps.action: Proposes that the Rahmiye fault is synchronized only in Phase III because of its position and trend as a graben boundary.
steps.quote: We assume this distinction is due to the Rahmiye fault acting as the eastern boundary of the Gediz-Alaşehir Graben

steps.action: Compares the recurrence intervals and slip rates with a literature compilation of Aegean, Italian and Israeli normal faults (Table 6) and tentatively infers 1 to 5 kyr recurrence.
steps.quote: we tentatively conclude that both the Aegean extensional region and Italy

steps.action: Checks the modeled average slip rates against the 'fanning pattern' of 584 concentration profiles and against theoretical rates from scarp height divided by LGM age; takes the agreement as evidence of tectonic exhumation.
steps.quote: The slip rates derived from the fault scarp modeling (SRm) are adequately consistent with this hypothesis

steps.action: Compares the geological slip rates with GPS-derived dip-slip rates (Reilinger 2006; Aktug 2009) and finds large discrepancies, attributed to strain partitioning and fluctuating strain release.
steps.quote: we made a brief comparison of short-term slip rate, using geodetic results of 17 years

steps.action: Concludes with at least 20 events on seven faults, four synchronous phases, about 2000-year regional recurrence, and slip rates increasing through the late Holocene.
steps.quote: Four synchronous phases of activity at around 2, 4, 6, and 8 ka indicate a recurrence interval of ca. 2000 years

end.claim: At least 20 seismic events over the past 16 kyr on seven western Anatolian faults, with ages and slips (0.6–4.2 m) given with uncertainties, group into four regional activity phases at ca. 8, 6, 4 and 2 ka (recurrence ca. 2000 yr), with incremental slip rates from >0.1 to 2.2 mm/yr.

decisive_move.sentence: The FSDT Monte Carlo inversion of the 214 new 36Cl concentrations into event ages and slips, with scenario selection by fit statistics, is the step without which no event history would exist.

gates.evidence: Sampling was directed by the method's premise (episodic exhumation recorded in 36Cl, §1 ¶3) and by choosing key boundary faults (§1 ¶4), not by a rival hypothesis. The modeled histories faced checks they could have failed: plausibility against length-based magnitudes (§6 ¶1), the fanning pattern and theoretical slip rates (§7.3 ¶1), and weathering and archaeological evidence (§6 ¶2). The magnitude check failed for a 7 km Rahmiye fault and was absorbed by revising the fault length (§5.4 ¶1). The activity phases were grouped after the ages were seen (§7.1 ¶2). Selection criteria (lowest chi-square/RMSw/AICc) and the 20 cm ground-line uncertainty are stated in Methods (§4.4 ¶4), but nothing indicates they were fixed before the data.

36Cl production rates by spallation, neutron capture and muons; scaling schemes
Random-walk Monte Carlo search of rupture-history parameter space
Model selection by chi-square, weighted RMS and Akaike information criterion (AICc)
ICP and ICP-MS determination of major and trace elements
Roman-age attribution of chisel marks used as a relative age constraint on exhumation

novelty_claims.quote: we improved the seismic datasets of western Anatolia based on cosmogenic 36Cl by studying two new major faults in detail
Our finding reveals high capability of cosmogenic 36Cl dating to explore seismic behavior of active faults beyond the existing earthquake records.
the cross-cutting relationships of ancient excavation and vertical dissolution mark can be used as a simple but fascinating tool

limits: No peer-review file or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: the four regional activity phases and the ca. 2000-year regional recurrence are best_explanation (grouped by time correlation from P-CAAT peaks, explicitly 'merely an estimation', with spatial connection unknown, §7.1 ¶2); the interpretation of events as earthquake clusters of M 6.5–7.1 is best_explanation (§6 ¶3); the Aegean and Italy recurrence of 1–5 kyr is a tentative regularity_in_range from a literature compilation (§7.2 ¶2); the Rahmiye–Akselendi linkage is an inference that protects the modeled slips (§5.4 ¶1). Only one code (FSDT) was used; comparison with other codes is declared beyond scope (§4.4 ¶1). The scenario fit tables (Table S7) and modeling details are in the supplement, which was not supplied. The five earlier faults are inherited reconstructions; the paper reanalyses their slip rates, apparently without re-running the age models (inference from §1 ¶4 and §2). Whether the phase grouping or the selection criteria were fixed before seeing results is not reported. The geodetic discrepancy is noted but left unexplained (§7.3 ¶2).

disagreements.target: Geodetic dip-slip rates of Reilinger et al. (2006) and Aktug et al. (2009)
disagreements.support: Geological incremental slip rates (>0.1–2.2 mm/yr) are far below the GPS rates (14.5–20.2 and 1.3–6.6 mm/yr); the authors attribute this to strain partitioning among segments and fluctuating strain release.
disagreements.quote: Only, the lower limit of slip rates derived from geodetic data (Aktug et al., 3) are to some degree consistent with incremental slip rates

disagreements.target: Authors' earlier slip rates for the Kalafat, Yavansu and Priene-Sazlı faults (Mozafari et al. 2019a, 2019b)
disagreements.support: Slip rates are recalculated using modeled throw (maximum vertical displacement) and elapsed time since the latest event, instead of dip-slip on the fault surface.
disagreements.quote: Slip rate values of the last three faults above are recalculated with regards to modeled throw/maximum vertical displacement instead of considering dip-slip values
